Extraction: Co-Evolving Multi-Agent Transfer Reinforcement Learning via Scenario Independent Representation
Ayesha Siddiqua; Siming Liu; Ayesha Siddika Nipu; Anthony Harris; Yan Liu

Not an IT-operations paper: it targets the difficulty of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) in Multi-Agent Systems, where learning complex cooperative/competitive tasks from scratch is "challenging and often unfeasible" for large numbers of agents due to exponential state expansion, scenario-dependent state sizes that block knowledge transfer, and static built-in AI opponents that cap further policy improvement (Abstract; Sec. I, pp. 99439-99440).

Co-MACTRL: a co-evolutionary curriculum transfer learning framework for MARL (no LLMs, no copilot, no human-in-the-loop). Uses scenario-independent state/action representations via Agent Influence Maps (64x64 Multi-Agent Influence Map for abstracted global info; 37x37 local IM) feeding fixed-size A3C actor-critic MLPs (two hidden layers of 64 neurons) under Centralized Training with Semi-Centralized Execution (CTSCE); attack action generalized to the closest enemy. Curriculum sequence 3m -> 8m -> 2s3z -> 3s5z, then an arena of three MARL learners co-evolving against static built-in AI and each other on multi-player enabled SMAC (MP-SMAC, map 3s5z_mp) (Sec. III-A to III-D, pp. 99442-99446; Algorithms 1-2).

Simulation-based controlled experiments in the StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC) and the authors' extended MP-SMAC (StarCraft II). Results collected from 7 different random seeds, experiments up to 80 million steps, evaluation every 25 game episodes; CTL uses 1M steps per map; evaluation matrix runs 32 distinct game episodes per map per phase; Co-MACTRL trained 72M game steps over four cycles with three learners; compared against baseline MARL (3s5z from scratch) and Co-MARL without CTL (Sec. III-B.2, p. 99444; Sec. III-D, pp. 99445-99446; Sec. IV-A/B, pp. 99447-99449).

Not applicable — a game-based MARL study; no MTTD, MTTR, alert fatigue, or incident-resolution metrics are reported anywhere in the paper (entire paper; results are win rates in StarCraft II scenarios, Sec. IV, pp. 99446-99449).

Field: General Impact on Agentic AI / Multi-Agent Systems
Extraction: MACTRL (CTL) learner reached 87% win rate on 3m, 68% on 8m, 85% on 2s3z, and 85% early on 3s5z vs. 72% for the regular learner in 8M steps; "the MACTRL learner outperforms regular MARL learner by an average of 50% across all four scenarios"; highest average win rate 80%. Co-MACTRL learners surpass MACTRL peak values by nearly 7%; over cycles, 3m win rate rose 80%->90% and 8m 60%->73%; Co-MARL without CTL averaged nearly 50% lower on unseen maps. Failure mode: continued training on 3s5z degrades performance on earlier maps after 7M steps (forgetting); learners exhibit an emergent generalized "focus fire" strategy (Sec. IV-A/B/C, Tables 2-3, Figs. 4-6, pp. 99446-99449).

Authors state testing "was confined to a restricted set of scenarios"; future work: evaluate on a broader spectrum of heterogeneous environments with more intricate maps, explore more advanced curriculum learning designs and knowledge transfer approaches for co-evolutionary MARL, and integrate additional deep RL techniques such as recurrent neural networks (Sec. V, p. 99450).

This paper is tangential to Agentic AI copilots for incident response: it contains no LLMs, observability, AIOps, or incident metrics. Its value to the thesis is conceptual — it demonstrates multi-agent coordination mechanisms (shared reward, centralized training with abstracted global state) and shows that curriculum transfer and co-evolution let agent teams reuse knowledge across scenarios instead of learning from scratch, a principle analogous to transferring incident-handling knowledge across incident types. The scenario-independent state representation idea could inform how an incident-response agent normalizes heterogeneous telemetry into a fixed input. The reported forgetting when training shifts to new scenarios is a cautionary finding for continuously learning ops agents. Overall it can only support background discussion of multi-agent learning, not the MTTD/MTTR evidence base.
Low — a game-based MARL/transfer-learning study with no incident response, AIOps, LLM, or MTTD/MTTR content; only tangentially relevant as multi-agent systems background.
